#In brief

  • A function assigns to every xxx in the domain one and only one value f(x)f(x)f(x): on the graph, every vertical line meets the curve at most once.
  • Domain: exclude the zeros of the denominators and require radicand ≥0\ge 0≥0 in roots of even index (>0> 0>0 if the root is in a denominator); roots of odd index impose no conditions.
  • The zeros of fff are the solutions of f(x)=0f(x) = 0f(x)=0, that is the xxx-coordinates of the points where the graph crosses the xxx-axis.
  • Injective: different values of xxx give different values. Surjective: the range is the whole codomain. Bijective means both, that is invertible; the graph of f−1f^{-1}f−1 is symmetric to that of fff with respect to the line y=xy = xy=x.
  • Composite: (g∘f)(x)=g(f(x))(g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x))(g∘f)(x)=g(f(x)), first fff and then ggg; in general g∘f≠f∘gg \circ f \ne f \circ gg∘f=f∘g.
  • Even: f(−x)=f(x)f(-x) = f(x)f(−x)=f(x), graph symmetric with respect to the yyy-axis. Odd: f(−x)=−f(x)f(-x) = -f(x)f(−x)=−f(x), symmetric with respect to the origin. Periodic: f(x+T)=f(x)f(x + T) = f(x)f(x+T)=f(x).
  • Translations (with c>0c > 0c>0): f(x−c)f(x - c)f(x−c) shifts the graph to the right, f(x+c)f(x + c)f(x+c) to the left, f(x)+cf(x) + cf(x)+c up, f(x)−cf(x) - cf(x)−c down.
  • Functions to recognise at a glance: constant, piecewise, ∣x∣|x|∣x∣ and ∣f(x)∣|f(x)|∣f(x)∣, linear y=mx+qy = mx + qy=mx+q (direct proportionality if q=0q = 0q=0 and m≠0m \ne 0m=0), y=kxy = \frac{k}{x}y=xk​ (inverse proportionality).

#6.1 Definition of a function and main features

#Definition and terminology

Definition 6.1 Function

A function fff from a set AAA to a set BBB is a rule that assigns to every element xxx of AAA one and only one element of BBB, denoted by f(x)f(x)f(x). You write

f:A→B,x↦f(x)f: A \to B, \qquad x \mapsto f(x)f:A→B,x↦f(x)

and read “fff from AAA to BBB, which maps xxx to f(x)f(x)f(x)”. Here AAA and BBB are subsets of R\RR, the set of real numbers: we speak of real functions of a real variable. You often write y=f(x)y = f(x)y=f(x).

The names you need to know:

  • AAA is the domain, BBB the codomain (the target set).
  • xxx is the independent variable, y=f(x)y = f(x)y=f(x) the dependent variable, because its value depends on xxx through the rule.
  • f(x)f(x)f(x) is the image of xxx. The range (image) of the whole function, f(A)f(A)f(A), is the set of the values it takes: it can be smaller than the codomain.
  • The preimage (controimmagine) of a value yyy is the set of the xxx in the domain for which f(x)=yf(x) = yf(x)=y: it can contain a single element, several elements, or none (it is then the empty set, ∅\emptyset∅).
Example 6.1 Images and preimages for f(x)=x2f(x) = x^2f(x)=x2

With f:R→Rf: \R \to \Rf:R→R, f(x)=x2f(x) = x^2f(x)=x2: the image of 333 is f(3)=9f(3) = 9f(3)=9. The preimage of 444 is {−2,2}\{-2, 2\}{−2,2} (two elements), that of 000 is {0}\{0\}{0}, that of −1-1−1 is empty, because no square is negative. The range of fff is [0,+∞)[0, +\infty)[0,+∞), smaller than the codomain R\RR.

Other examples: the graph of f(x)=3x−1f(x) = 3x - 1f(x)=3x−1 is a line (linear function); the graph of f(x)=x2−2xf(x) = x^2 - 2xf(x)=x2−2x is a parabola (second-degree polynomial function); f:N→Nf: \N \to \Nf:N→N, f(n)=2nf(n) = 2nf(n)=2n assigns to every natural number its double, and its range, the set of even numbers, is smaller than the codomain N\NN.

Note Algebraic and transcendental functions

Algebraic functions are built from polynomials with sums, differences, products, quotients and extraction of roots: they are the ones in this module. The others are called transcendental: exponentials, logarithms and trigonometric functions, which have their own modules. The properties that follow hold for all of them.

#The domain

When a function is given only by a formula, its domain (in Italian also campo di esistenza) is the set of real numbers for which the formula makes sense.

Method Domain conditions (condizioni di esistenza)
  • Fraction: the denominator must be ≠0\ne 0=0.
  • Root of even index (  \sqrt{\;}​,   4\sqrt[4]{\;}4​, …): radicand ≥0\ge 0≥0.
  • Root of even index in a denominator: radicand >0> 0>0 (it must be ≥0\ge 0≥0 and also ≠0\ne 0=0).
  • Root of odd index (  3\sqrt[3]{\;}3​, …): no condition on the radicand.
  • If there are several conditions, they must all hold together: you put them into a system.

Logarithms and exponentials have their own rules, which you will see together with those functions.

Example 6.2 Six domains
  • f(x)=x+1x2−4f(x) = \frac{x + 1}{x^2 - 4}f(x)=x2−4x+1​: x2−4≠0x^2 - 4 \ne 0x2−4=0, so x≠2x \ne 2x=2 and x≠−2x \ne -2x=−2. Domain R∖{−2,2}\R \setminus \{-2, 2\}R∖{−2,2}, which reads “R\RR minus −2-2−2 and 222”.
  • f(x)=6−2xf(x) = \sqrt{6 - 2x}f(x)=6−2x​: 6−2x≥06 - 2x \ge 06−2x≥0, that is x≤3x \le 3x≤3. Domain (−∞,3](-\infty, 3](−∞,3].
  • f(x)=x2−5x+6f(x) = \sqrt{x^2 - 5x + 6}f(x)=x2−5x+6​: (x−2)(x−3)≥0(x - 2)(x - 3) \ge 0(x−2)(x−3)≥0; the parabola opens upwards, so x≤2x \le 2x≤2 or x≥3x \ge 3x≥3.
  • f(x)=xx−4f(x) = \frac{\sqrt{x}}{x - 4}f(x)=x−4x​​: x≥0x \ge 0x≥0 and x≠4x \ne 4x=4. Domain [0,4)∪(4,+∞)[0, 4) \cup (4, +\infty)[0,4)∪(4,+∞).
  • f(x)=1x+3f(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x + 3}}f(x)=x+3​1​: root in a denominator, so x+3>0x + 3 > 0x+3>0, that is x>−3x > -3x>−3.
  • f(x)=x−13f(x) = \sqrt[3]{x - 1}f(x)=3x−1​: cube root, no condition. Domain R\RR.
Common mistake Find the domain before simplifying

f(x)=x2−1x−1f(x) = \frac{x^2 - 1}{x - 1}f(x)=x−1x2−1​ has domain x≠1x \ne 1x=1. Simplifying gives x+1x + 1x+1, but the value x=1x = 1x=1 remains excluded: the graph is the line y=x+1y = x + 1y=x+1 without the point (1,2)(1, 2)(1,2). Also remember that the conditions from a denominator and from a root hold together (“and”), not as alternatives.

#Zeros and sign of a function

A number ccc is a zero of fff if f(c)=0f(c) = 0f(c)=0. Finding the zeros is the same as solving the equation f(x)=0f(x) = 0f(x)=0, that is the system of y=f(x)y = f(x)y=f(x) and y=0y = 0y=0: graphically, the zeros are the xxx-coordinates of the points where the graph crosses the xxx-axis. In the same way, f(x)>0f(x) > 0f(x)>0 where the graph lies above the xxx-axis and f(x)<0f(x) < 0f(x)<0 where it lies below; the solutions of f(x)=g(x)f(x) = g(x)f(x)=g(x) are the xxx-coordinates of the points the two graphs have in common. The graph crosses the yyy-axis at the point (0,f(0))(0, f(0))(0,f(0)), if 000 is in the domain.

Example 6.3 Zeros and sign of a polynomial

f(x)=x3−x2−6xf(x) = x^3 - x^2 - 6xf(x)=x3−x2−6x. Take out the common factor xxx and factorise the trinomial: f(x)=x(x2−x−6)=x(x−3)(x+2)f(x) = x(x^2 - x - 6) = x(x - 3)(x + 2)f(x)=x(x2−x−6)=x(x−3)(x+2). The zeros are −2-2−2, 000 and 333. With the sign study of the factors: f(x)>0f(x) > 0f(x)>0 for −2<x<0-2 < x < 0−2<x<0 or x>3x > 3x>3; f(x)<0f(x) < 0f(x)<0 for x<−2x < -2x<−2 or 0<x<30 < x < 30<x<3.

Common mistake The zeros must be in the domain

f(x)=x2−4x−2f(x) = \frac{x^2 - 4}{x - 2}f(x)=x−2x2−4​: the numerator is zero for x=2x = 2x=2 and for x=−2x = -2x=−2, but x=2x = 2x=2 is excluded from the domain. The only zero is x=−2x = -2x=−2.

#Graph of a function

Definition 6.2 Graph

The graph of fff is the set of the points (x,f(x))(x, f(x))(x,f(x)) of the plane, with xxx in the domain. A curve is the graph of a function if and only if every vertical line meets it in at most one point: two points on the same vertical line would mean two values for the same xxx.

From the graph you can read the domain, by projecting the curve onto the xxx-axis, and the range, by projecting it onto the yyy-axis.

Example 6.4 Circle and semicircle

The circle x2+y2=4x^2 + y^2 = 4x2+y2=4 is not the graph of a function: the line x=1x = 1x=1 meets it at (1,3)(1, \sqrt3)(1,3​) and at (1,−3)(1, -\sqrt3)(1,−3​). The upper semicircle y=4−x2y = \sqrt{4 - x^2}y=4−x2​, on the other hand, is a function, with domain [−2,2][-2, 2][−2,2] (you need 4−x2≥04 - x^2 \ge 04−x2≥0) and range [0,2][0, 2][0,2].

#Injective, surjective and bijective functions

Definition 6.3 Injective, surjective, bijective
  • fff is injective if distinct elements of the domain have distinct images: x1≠x2⇒f(x1)≠f(x2)x_1 \ne x_2 \Rightarrow f(x_1) \ne f(x_2)x1​=x2​⇒f(x1​)=f(x2​) (the arrow ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ reads “implies”). Equivalently: f(x1)=f(x2)⇒x1=x2f(x_1) = f(x_2) \Rightarrow x_1 = x_2f(x1​)=f(x2​)⇒x1​=x2​. An injective function never takes the same value twice.
  • f:A→Bf: A \to Bf:A→B is surjective if every element of the codomain is the image of at least one element of the domain: for every y∈By \in By∈B there exists x∈Ax \in Ax∈A with f(x)=yf(x) = yf(x)=y (the symbol ∈\in∈ reads “belongs to”). In other words f(A)=Bf(A) = Bf(A)=B.
  • fff is bijective (in Italian biiettiva or biunivoca) if it is both injective and surjective: there is a one-to-one correspondence between domain and codomain.

On the graph you look at the horizontal lines y=ky = ky=k, with kkk in the codomain: fff is injective if each of them meets the graph at most once, surjective if each of them meets it at least once, bijective if exactly once.

Example 6.5 Four cases
  • f(x)=5x−2f(x) = 5x - 2f(x)=5x−2, from R\RR to R\RR: injective, because 5x1−2=5x2−25x_1 - 2 = 5x_2 - 25x1​−2=5x2​−2 implies x1=x2x_1 = x_2x1​=x2​; surjective, because for every yyy you just take x=y+25x = \frac{y + 2}{5}x=5y+2​. It is bijective, like every non-horizontal line.
  • f(x)=x2f(x) = x^2f(x)=x2, from R\RR to R\RR: it is not injective (f(−2)=f(2)=4f(-2) = f(2) = 4f(−2)=f(2)=4: to disprove it, a single counterexample is enough) and it is not surjective (negative values are never taken). If you take [0,+∞)[0, +\infty)[0,+∞) as the codomain it becomes surjective: surjectivity depends on the chosen codomain.
  • f(x)=x3f(x) = x^3f(x)=x3, from R\RR to R\RR: bijective; every horizontal line cuts the graph exactly once.
  • f(x)=1xf(x) = \frac{1}{x}f(x)=x1​, from R∖{0}\R \setminus \{0\}R∖{0} to R\RR: injective but not surjective, because the value 000 is never taken.

#Restriction of a function

Definition 6.4 Restriction

If D⊆AD \subseteq AD⊆A (DDD is contained in AAA), the restriction of fff to DDD is the function f∣D:D→Bf|_D: D \to Bf∣D​:D→B that acts like fff but only on the points of DDD: f∣D(x)=f(x)f|_D(x) = f(x)f∣D​(x)=f(x) for every x∈Dx \in Dx∈D. The domain is restricted; the codomain stays the same.

It is used above all to obtain an injective function: x2x^2x2 is not injective on R\RR, but its restrictions to [0,+∞)[0, +\infty)[0,+∞) and to (−∞,0](-\infty, 0](−∞,0] are.

#Inverse function

Definition 6.5 Inverse function

If f:A→Bf: A \to Bf:A→B is bijective, its inverse f−1:B→Af^{-1}: B \to Af−1:B→A (read “fff inverse” or “fff to the minus one”) assigns to every y∈By \in By∈B the unique x∈Ax \in Ax∈A such that f(x)=yf(x) = yf(x)=y. So f−1(f(x))=xf^{-1}(f(x)) = xf−1(f(x))=x and f(f−1(y))=yf(f^{-1}(y)) = yf(f−1(y))=y: the dependent variable of fff becomes the independent variable of f−1f^{-1}f−1. A function is invertible if and only if it is bijective, and the domain of f−1f^{-1}f−1 is the range of fff. The graph of f−1f^{-1}f−1 is symmetric to that of fff with respect to the bisector y=xy = xy=x.

Method Computing the inverse
  1. Check that fff is bijective; if it is not, restrict the domain (and take the range as the codomain).
  2. Write y=f(x)y = f(x)y=f(x) and solve for xxx in terms of yyy.
  3. Swap the names of the variables, to go back to the usual notation with xxx as the independent variable.
  4. Check that f(f−1(x))=xf(f^{-1}(x)) = xf(f−1(x))=x.
Example 6.6 Inverse of a linear function

f(x)=2x−6f(x) = 2x - 6f(x)=2x−6, from R\RR to R\RR. From y=2x−6y = 2x - 6y=2x−6 you get x=y+62x = \frac{y + 6}{2}x=2y+6​; swapping the names, f−1(x)=x2+3f^{-1}(x) = \frac{x}{2} + 3f−1(x)=2x​+3. Check: f(x2+3)=2(x2+3)−6=xf\left(\frac{x}{2} + 3\right) = 2\left(\frac{x}{2} + 3\right) - 6 = xf(2x​+3)=2(2x​+3)−6=x. The point (3,0)(3, 0)(3,0) of the graph of fff becomes the point (0,3)(0, 3)(0,3) of the graph of f−1f^{-1}f−1; the two lines meet on the bisector, at (6,6)(6, 6)(6,6).

Example 6.7 Inverting after a restriction

f(x)=x2f(x) = x^2f(x)=x2 is not invertible on R\RR. The restriction to [0,+∞)[0, +\infty)[0,+∞), with codomain [0,+∞)[0, +\infty)[0,+∞), is bijective: from y=x2y = x^2y=x2 with x≥0x \ge 0x≥0 you get x=yx = \sqrt{y}x=y​, so the inverse is x\sqrt{x}x​. The restriction to (−∞,0](-\infty, 0](−∞,0], instead, has inverse −x-\sqrt{x}−x​.

Common mistake f−1f^{-1}f−1 is not 1f\frac{1}{f}f1​

Here the exponent −1-1−1 does not denote the reciprocal: for f(x)=2x−6f(x) = 2x - 6f(x)=2x−6 the inverse is x2+3\frac{x}{2} + 32x​+3, whereas 1f(x)=12x−6\frac{1}{f(x)} = \frac{1}{2x - 6}f(x)1​=2x−61​ is a completely different function.

#Composition of functions

Definition 6.6 Composite function

Given f:A→Bf: A \to Bf:A→B and g:B→Cg: B \to Cg:B→C, the composite g∘fg \circ fg∘f (read “ggg composed with fff”) is the function from AAA to CCC defined by

(g∘f)(x)=g(f(x))(g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x))(g∘f)(x)=g(f(x))

You apply fff first (the inner function) and then ggg (the outer function). For this to be possible, the range of fff must be contained in the domain of ggg; if it is not, you restrict the domain of fff.

Example 6.8 The order matters

f(x)=2x+1f(x) = 2x + 1f(x)=2x+1 and g(x)=x2−3g(x) = x^2 - 3g(x)=x2−3. (g∘f)(x)=g(2x+1)=(2x+1)2−3=4x2+4x−2(g \circ f)(x) = g(2x + 1) = (2x + 1)^2 - 3 = 4x^2 + 4x - 2(g∘f)(x)=g(2x+1)=(2x+1)2−3=4x2+4x−2. (f∘g)(x)=f(x2−3)=2(x2−3)+1=2x2−5(f \circ g)(x) = f(x^2 - 3) = 2(x^2 - 3) + 1 = 2x^2 - 5(f∘g)(x)=f(x2−3)=2(x2−3)+1=2x2−5. At a point: (g∘f)(1)=g(f(1))=g(3)=6(g \circ f)(1) = g(f(1)) = g(3) = 6(g∘f)(1)=g(f(1))=g(3)=6, whereas (f∘g)(1)=f(g(1))=f(−2)=−3(f \circ g)(1) = f(g(1)) = f(-2) = -3(f∘g)(1)=f(g(1))=f(−2)=−3.

Example 6.9 Composites and domain

f(x)=x−3f(x) = x - 3f(x)=x−3 and g(x)=xg(x) = \sqrt{x}g(x)=x​. The composite (g∘f)(x)=x−3(g \circ f)(x) = \sqrt{x - 3}(g∘f)(x)=x−3​ exists only for x≥3x \ge 3x≥3: you must restrict fff to [3,+∞)[3, +\infty)[3,+∞), where f(x)≥0f(x) \ge 0f(x)≥0. The other one, (f∘g)(x)=x−3(f \circ g)(x) = \sqrt{x} - 3(f∘g)(x)=x​−3, has domain x≥0x \ge 0x≥0.

Being able to recognise a composite is useful: h(x)=(3x−1)5h(x) = (3x - 1)^5h(x)=(3x−1)5 is g(f(x))g(f(x))g(f(x)) with f(x)=3x−1f(x) = 3x - 1f(x)=3x−1 and g(t)=t5g(t) = t^5g(t)=t5. You can also compose three or more functions, always starting from the innermost one.

Common mistake Composite, not product

(g∘f)(x)(g \circ f)(x)(g∘f)(x) is read from right to left: fff first. And it is not the product g(x)⋅f(x)g(x) \cdot f(x)g(x)⋅f(x): with f(x)=x−1f(x) = x - 1f(x)=x−1 and g(x)=x2g(x) = x^2g(x)=x2 you have (g∘f)(x)=(x−1)2(g \circ f)(x) = (x - 1)^2(g∘f)(x)=(x−1)2, whereas g(x)⋅f(x)=x3−x2g(x) \cdot f(x) = x^3 - x^2g(x)⋅f(x)=x3−x2.

#Even and odd functions

Definition 6.7 Even and odd

The domain must be symmetric with respect to 000: if it contains xxx, it also contains −x-x−x.

  • fff is even if f(−x)=f(x)f(-x) = f(x)f(−x)=f(x) for every xxx in the domain: the graph is symmetric with respect to the yyy-axis.
  • fff is odd if f(−x)=−f(x)f(-x) = -f(x)f(−x)=−f(x) for every xxx in the domain: the graph is symmetric with respect to the origin.

The names come from polynomials: those with only even powers of xxx (constants count as even powers), such as x2x^2x2 or x4−3x2+2x^4 - 3x^2 + 2x4−3x2+2, are even; those with only odd powers, such as xxx or x3−3xx^3 - 3xx3−3x, are odd. But there are many even or odd functions that are not polynomials: ∣x∣|x|∣x∣ and cos⁡x\cos xcosx are even, 1x\frac{1}{x}x1​ and sin⁡x\sin xsinx are odd. Most functions are neither even nor odd. If an odd function is defined at 000, then f(0)=0f(0) = 0f(0)=0. Knowing that a function is even or odd lets you study it only for x≥0x \ge 0x≥0 and obtain the rest by symmetry.

Method Deciding whether a function is even or odd
  1. Check that the domain is symmetric; if it is not, the function is neither even nor odd.
  2. Compute f(−x)f(-x)f(−x) by putting −x-x−x in place of every xxx, and simplify.
  3. If you get back f(x)f(x)f(x) it is even; if you get −f(x)-f(x)−f(x) it is odd; otherwise it is neither (to show this, one value is enough, for example x=1x = 1x=1).
Example 6.10 Four checks
  • f(x)=x4−3x2+2f(x) = x^4 - 3x^2 + 2f(x)=x4−3x2+2: f(−x)=(−x)4−3(−x)2+2=x4−3x2+2=f(x)f(-x) = (-x)^4 - 3(-x)^2 + 2 = x^4 - 3x^2 + 2 = f(x)f(−x)=(−x)4−3(−x)2+2=x4−3x2+2=f(x), even.
  • h(x)=xx2+1h(x) = \frac{x}{x^2 + 1}h(x)=x2+1x​: h(−x)=−xx2+1=−h(x)h(-x) = \frac{-x}{x^2 + 1} = -h(x)h(−x)=x2+1−x​=−h(x), odd.
  • k(x)=x2−2xk(x) = x^2 - 2xk(x)=x2−2x: k(−x)=x2+2xk(-x) = x^2 + 2xk(−x)=x2+2x, which is neither k(x)k(x)k(x) nor −k(x)-k(x)−k(x) (for example k(1)=−1k(1) = -1k(1)=−1 and k(−1)=3k(-1) = 3k(−1)=3): neither even nor odd.
  • x2−4\sqrt{x^2 - 4}x2−4​ is even, with the symmetric domain x≤−2x \le -2x≤−2 or x≥2x \ge 2x≥2; x−1\sqrt{x - 1}x−1​ is neither even nor odd, because its domain [1,+∞)[1, +\infty)[1,+∞) is not symmetric.
Common mistake “Not even” does not mean “odd”

There are three possibilities, not two: even, odd, neither (the only function that is both even and odd is the one that is always 000). And watch the signs: (−x)3=−x3(-x)^3 = -x^3(−x)3=−x3 but (−x)2=x2(-x)^2 = x^2(−x)2=x2, whereas −x2-x^2−x2 means −(x2)-(x^2)−(x2).

#Periodic functions

Definition 6.8 Periodic function

fff is periodic with period T>0T > 0T>0 if f(x+T)=f(x)f(x + T) = f(x)f(x+T)=f(x) for every xxx in the domain, and TTT is the smallest positive number with this property. The graph repeats identically every TTT: it is enough to study it on an interval of length TTT.

Consequently f(x+2T)=f(x)f(x + 2T) = f(x)f(x+2T)=f(x), f(x−T)=f(x)f(x - T) = f(x)f(x−T)=f(x) and in general f(x+nT)=f(x)f(x + nT) = f(x)f(x+nT)=f(x) for every integer nnn. The typical examples are the trigonometric functions: sin⁡x\sin xsinx and cos⁡x\cos xcosx have period 2π2\pi2π.

Example 6.11 Using the period

fff has period 333 and f(1)=5f(1) = 5f(1)=5. Then f(4)=f(1+3)=5f(4) = f(1 + 3) = 5f(4)=f(1+3)=5, f(10)=f(1+3⋅3)=5f(10) = f(1 + 3 \cdot 3) = 5f(10)=f(1+3⋅3)=5 and f(−2)=f(1−3)=5f(-2) = f(1 - 3) = 5f(−2)=f(1−3)=5.

Note The period of f(kx)f(kx)f(kx)

If fff has period TTT, then f(kx)f(kx)f(kx) has period T∣k∣\frac{T}{|k|}∣k∣T​: sin⁡(2x)\sin(2x)sin(2x) has period π\piπ, cos⁡(x2)\cos\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)cos(2x​) has period 4π4\pi4π. A translation, on the other hand, does not change the period.

#Increasing, decreasing and monotonic functions

Definition 6.9 Monotonicity on an interval III of the domain

For every x1,x2∈Ix_1, x_2 \in Ix1​,x2​∈I with x1<x2x_1 < x_2x1​<x2​:

  • fff is increasing on III if f(x1)<f(x2)f(x_1) < f(x_2)f(x1​)<f(x2​): the graph, traced from left to right, goes up;
  • fff is decreasing on III if f(x1)>f(x2)f(x_1) > f(x_2)f(x1​)>f(x2​): the graph goes down;
  • fff is non-decreasing on III if f(x1)≤f(x2)f(x_1) \le f(x_2)f(x1​)≤f(x2​), non-increasing if f(x1)≥f(x2)f(x_1) \ge f(x_2)f(x1​)≥f(x2​): horizontal pieces are allowed.

A function that has one of these properties on III is called monotonic on III. Some books call “strictly increasing” what is called increasing here, and “increasing” what is called non-decreasing here.

Example 6.12 Intervals of monotonicity
  • y=mx+qy = mx + qy=mx+q: increasing on the whole of R\RR if m>0m > 0m>0, decreasing if m<0m < 0m<0; if m=0m = 0m=0 it is constant, that is non-increasing and non-decreasing at the same time.
  • f(x)=x2−6x+5f(x) = x^2 - 6x + 5f(x)=x2−6x+5: parabola opening upwards with vertex (3,−4)(3, -4)(3,−4). It is decreasing on (−∞,3](-\infty, 3](−∞,3] and increasing on [3,+∞)[3, +\infty)[3,+∞); it is not monotonic on the whole of R\RR.
Common mistake Monotonic piece by piece does not mean monotonic

f(x)=1xf(x) = \frac{1}{x}f(x)=x1​ is decreasing on (−∞,0)(-\infty, 0)(−∞,0) and on (0,+∞)(0, +\infty)(0,+∞), but not on its whole domain: −1<1-1 < 1−1<1 and also f(−1)=−1<f(1)=1f(-1) = -1 < f(1) = 1f(−1)=−1<f(1)=1. The intervals of monotonicity must be given separately.

A function that is increasing (or decreasing) on its whole domain is injective: this is a convenient way to show that it is invertible.

#Bounded functions

Definition 6.10 Bounded function
  • fff is bounded above if there is a number KKK such that f(x)≤Kf(x) \le Kf(x)≤K for every xxx in the domain;
  • fff is bounded below if there is a number KKK such that f(x)≥Kf(x) \ge Kf(x)≥K for every xxx in the domain;
  • fff is bounded if it is both bounded above and bounded below: its graph lies entirely within a horizontal strip of the plane.
Example 6.13 Bounded and unbounded
  • sin⁡x\sin xsinx and cos⁡x\cos xcosx take values between −1-1−1 and 111: they are bounded. Consequently cos⁡x+1\cos x + 1cosx+1, which has values between 000 and 222, is bounded too.
  • x2x^2x2 is bounded below (x2≥0x^2 \ge 0x2≥0) but not above.
  • x3x^3x3 and 1x\frac{1}{x}x1​ are bounded neither above nor below.
  • f(x)=1x2+1f(x) = \frac{1}{x^2 + 1}f(x)=x2+11​: the denominator is at least 111, so 0<f(x)≤10 < f(x) \le 10<f(x)≤1. It is bounded, and the value 111, reached at x=0x = 0x=0, is its maximum.

#Continuous functions

A precise definition of continuity requires the tools of mathematical analysis; here the intuitive idea is enough: a function is continuous on an interval if its graph, on that interval, can be drawn without lifting the pen from the paper. Lines, parabolas, polynomials, ∣x∣|x|∣x∣ and x\sqrt{x}x​ are continuous. The graph of 1x\frac{1}{x}x1​ has two branches because x=0x = 0x=0 is not in the domain, but each branch can be drawn without lifting the pen.

A function is discontinuous at a point of its domain when its graph “jumps” there. This often happens with piecewise functions and with quantities that are counted: the number of people in a room, as a function of time, changes in jumps; the temperature of the room, on the other hand, varies continuously.

Example 6.14 A jump

g(x)=2xg(x) = 2xg(x)=2x for x≤1x \le 1x≤1 and g(x)=x+3g(x) = x + 3g(x)=x+3 for x>1x > 1x>1. At x=1x = 1x=1 we have g(1)=2g(1) = 2g(1)=2, but just to the right of 111 the values are close to 1+3=41 + 3 = 41+3=4: the graph jumps from 222 to 444, and ggg is discontinuous at x=1x = 1x=1.

#Translations

Rule 6.1 Translating the graph of fff (with c>0c > 0c>0)
  • y=f(x−c)y = f(x - c)y=f(x−c): the graph of fff shifted to the right by ccc;
  • y=f(x+c)y = f(x + c)y=f(x+c): shifted to the left by ccc;
  • y=f(x)+cy = f(x) + cy=f(x)+c: shifted up by ccc;
  • y=f(x)−cy = f(x) - cy=f(x)−c: shifted down by ccc.

If the constant is inside the argument, the translation is horizontal and goes “against” the sign; if it is outside, it is vertical and follows the sign. Together: y=f(x−h)+ky = f(x - h) + ky=f(x−h)+k is the graph of fff shifted by hhh horizontally and by kkk vertically.

Why “against”: in y=f(x−2)y = f(x - 2)y=f(x−2) the value that fff took at 000 is taken when x−2=0x - 2 = 0x−2=0, that is at x=2x = 2x=2. Everything happens 222 units further to the right.

Example 6.15 Three translations
  • y=(x−2)2+1y = (x - 2)^2 + 1y=(x−2)2+1: the parabola y=x2y = x^2y=x2 shifted 222 to the right and 111 up; the vertex moves from (0,0)(0, 0)(0,0) to (2,1)(2, 1)(2,1). Expanding: y=x2−4x+5y = x^2 - 4x + 5y=x2−4x+5, and indeed xV=42=2x_V = \frac{4}{2} = 2xV​=24​=2.
  • y=∣x+3∣−2y = |x + 3| - 2y=∣x+3∣−2: the graph of ∣x∣|x|∣x∣ shifted 333 to the left and 222 down; the vertex of the “V” is (−3,−2)(-3, -2)(−3,−2).
  • y=1x−1+2y = \frac{1}{x - 1} + 2y=x−11​+2: the graph of 1x\frac{1}{x}x1​ shifted 111 to the right and 222 up. The lines that the branches approach (the asymptotes) become x=1x = 1x=1 and y=2y = 2y=2; the domain is x≠1x \ne 1x=1 and the range is y≠2y \ne 2y=2.
Common mistake When there is a coefficient in front of xxx

The horizontal translation is read after taking out the coefficient of xxx: 2x−4=2(x−2)\sqrt{2x - 4} = \sqrt{2(x - 2)}2x−4​=2(x−2)​ is the graph of 2x\sqrt{2x}2x​ shifted 222 to the right, not 444. In the same way, if g(x)=cos⁡(x2)g(x) = \cos\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)g(x)=cos(2x​), the shift by ccc to the left is g(x+c)=cos⁡(x+c2)g(x + c) = \cos\left(\frac{x + c}{2}\right)g(x+c)=cos(2x+c​): so cos⁡(x2+1)=cos⁡(x+22)\cos\left(\frac{x}{2} + 1\right) = \cos\left(\frac{x + 2}{2}\right)cos(2x​+1)=cos(2x+2​) is obtained from cos⁡(x2)\cos\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)cos(2x​) by shifting it 222 to the left.

Note Symmetries

y=−f(x)y = -f(x)y=−f(x) is symmetric to the graph of fff with respect to the xxx-axis; y=f(−x)y = f(-x)y=f(−x) is symmetric to it with respect to the yyy-axis. An even function coincides with f(−x)f(-x)f(−x); for an odd one f(−x)=−f(x)f(-x) = -f(x)f(−x)=−f(x).

In the test Functions in the test questions

In questions on the domain with a choice of four answers, try the “boundary” values of the options: a number that makes a denominator zero cannot be in the domain; a number that makes the radicand of an even root zero (not in a denominator) usually can. For even and odd, even in a multiple-choice question, compute f(−x)f(-x)f(−x) for each option, or compare f(1)f(1)f(1) and f(−1)f(-1)f(−1) to rule options out quickly. A composite evaluated at a point gives a number: compute the inner function first. For translations: inside the argument, against the sign; outside, following the sign.

#6.2 Examples of useful functions

#Constant function

Definition 6.11 Constant function

f:R→Rf: \R \to \Rf:R→R, f(x)=kf(x) = kf(x)=k, with kkk a fixed real number: all the elements of the domain have the same image kkk. The graph is the horizontal line y=ky = ky=k.

A constant function is even, bounded and not injective; its range is the single value kkk. For example f(x)=−2f(x) = -2f(x)=−2 is a negative constant function: its graph lies entirely below the xxx-axis.

#Piecewise functions

A function is piecewise-defined (definita a tratti) when it is given by different expressions on different intervals of the domain. It is written with a curly bracket:

f(x)={−x+1if x<1x2−1if x≥1f(x) = \begin{cases} -x + 1 & \text{if } x < 1 \\ x^2 - 1 & \text{if } x \ge 1 \end{cases}f(x)={−x+1x2−1​if x<1if x≥1​

To compute fff at a point, you first look at which interval xxx falls in, then use the formula of that piece: f(−2)=2+1=3f(-2) = 2 + 1 = 3f(−2)=2+1=3, f(0)=1f(0) = 1f(0)=1, f(1)=1−1=0f(1) = 1 - 1 = 0f(1)=1−1=0, f(2)=4−1=3f(2) = 4 - 1 = 3f(2)=4−1=3. The graph is a piece of a line for x<1x < 1x<1 and a piece of a parabola for x≥1x \ge 1x≥1; here the two pieces join at the point (1,0)(1, 0)(1,0) and the function is continuous. The range is [0,+∞)[0, +\infty)[0,+∞), and fff is not injective, because f(−2)=f(2)=3f(-2) = f(2) = 3f(−2)=f(2)=3.

Common mistake Overlapping conditions

The intervals of the pieces must not assign two different values to the same xxx. If two conditions include the same point (for example “x≤0x \le 0x≤0” and “x≥0x \ge 0x≥0”), the two formulas must give the same value there. To tell which piece an endpoint belongs to, look where the equals sign is.

#Absolute value function

Definition 6.12 Absolute value
f(x)=∣x∣={xif x≥0−xif x<0f(x) = |x| = \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0 \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0 \end{cases}f(x)=∣x∣={x−x​if x≥0if x<0​

The graph is a “V” with its vertex at the origin, made up of the bisector y=xy = xy=x for x≥0x \ge 0x≥0 and of y=−xy = -xy=−x for x<0x < 0x<0. The function is even, has range [0,+∞)[0, +\infty)[0,+∞), is decreasing on (−∞,0](-\infty, 0](−∞,0] and increasing on [0,+∞)[0, +\infty)[0,+∞).

Method Graph of y=∣f(x)∣y = |f(x)|y=∣f(x)∣
∣f(x)∣={f(x)where f(x)≥0−f(x)where f(x)<0|f(x)| = \begin{cases} f(x) & \text{where } f(x) \ge 0 \\ -f(x) & \text{where } f(x) < 0 \end{cases}∣f(x)∣={f(x)−f(x)​where f(x)≥0where f(x)<0​
  1. Draw the graph of y=f(x)y = f(x)y=f(x).
  2. Leave the part that lies above the xxx-axis (or on it) as it is.
  3. Flip the part that lies below upwards, symmetrically with respect to the xxx-axis.

The result never goes below the xxx-axis.

Example 6.16 y=∣x2−4∣y = |x^2 - 4|y=∣x2−4∣

The parabola y=x2−4y = x^2 - 4y=x2−4 lies below the xxx-axis for −2<x<2-2 < x < 2−2<x<2, with vertex (0,−4)(0, -4)(0,−4). Flipping that piece gives an arc with its highest point at (0,4)(0, 4)(0,4); outside [−2,2][-2, 2][−2,2] the graph does not change. The graph lets you count the solutions of ∣x2−4∣=k|x^2 - 4| = k∣x2−4∣=k: the line y=3y = 3y=3 cuts it at 444 points (x=±1x = \pm 1x=±1 and x=±7x = \pm\sqrt7x=±7​), the line y=4y = 4y=4 at 333 points (x=0x = 0x=0 and x=±22x = \pm 2\sqrt2x=±22​), the line y=5y = 5y=5 at 222 points (x=±3x = \pm 3x=±3).

#Linear function and direct proportionality

Definition 6.13 Linear function

f:R→Rf: \R \to \Rf:R→R, f(x)=mx+qf(x) = mx + qf(x)=mx+q, with mmm and qqq real: the graph is the line with slope mmm and yyy-intercept qqq. If q=0q = 0q=0 it becomes y=mxy = mxy=mx and the line passes through the origin.

Definition 6.14 Direct proportionality

Two quantities xxx and yyy are directly proportional if y=kxy = kxy=kx, with k≠0k \ne 0k=0 constant, that is if the ratio yx\frac{y}{x}xy​ is constant (for x≠0x \ne 0x=0). If xxx doubles, yyy doubles; if xxx triples, yyy triples. The number kkk is the constant of proportionality and the graph is a line through the origin.

Examples: the price of xxx notebooks at €333 each is y=3xy = 3xy=3x, with constant 333. In physics, from Newton's second law F=maF = maF=ma (force equals mass times acceleration) it follows that, for the same mass, the acceleration is directly proportional to the force: doubling the force doubles the acceleration.

Common mistake A line that does not pass through the origin is not proportionality

A taxi that costs €333 at the start plus €222 per kilometre has cost y=2x+3y = 2x + 3y=2x+3: the relation is linear, but doubling the kilometres does not double the cost (111 km costs €555, 222 km cost €777). It is not direct proportionality.

#The function 1x\frac{1}{x}x1​ and inverse proportionality

Definition 6.15 Inverse proportionality

Two quantities are inversely proportional if y=kxy = \frac{k}{x}y=xk​, with k≠0k \ne 0k=0 constant, that is if the product xy=kxy = kxy=k is constant. If xxx doubles, yyy halves. The simplest case is

f(x)=1x,x≠0f(x) = \frac{1}{x}, \qquad x \ne 0f(x)=x1​,x=0

whose graph is the rectangular hyperbola referred to its asymptotes, xy=1xy = 1xy=1: the asymptotes are the Cartesian axes.

Properties of 1x\frac{1}{x}x1​: domain and range R∖{0}\R \setminus \{0\}R∖{0}; odd; injective; decreasing on (−∞,0)(-\infty, 0)(−∞,0) and on (0,+∞)(0, +\infty)(0,+∞) taken separately; not bounded.

Example 6.17 Time and speed

To travel 120120120 km: at 606060 km/h you need 222 hours, at 404040 km/h 333 hours, at 120120120 km/h 111 hour. The product of speed and time is always 120120120: t=120vt = \frac{120}{v}t=v120​, inverse proportionality. The same goes for a=Fma = \frac{F}{m}a=mF​: for the same force, if the mass doubles the acceleration halves.

#Exercises

Exercise 6.1BasicDomains

Find the domain of: a) f(x)=2x+1x2−9f(x) = \frac{2x + 1}{x^2 - 9}f(x)=x2−92x+1​; b) g(x)=8−2xg(x) = \sqrt{8 - 2x}g(x)=8−2x​; c) h(x)=x−53x+1h(x) = \frac{\sqrt[3]{x - 5}}{x + 1}h(x)=x+13x−5​​; d) k(x)=x2−3x−4k(x) = \sqrt{x^2 - 3x - 4}k(x)=x2−3x−4​.

Solution
  • a) x2−9≠0x^2 - 9 \ne 0x2−9=0: x≠3x \ne 3x=3 and x≠−3x \ne -3x=−3. Domain R∖{−3,3}\R \setminus \{-3, 3\}R∖{−3,3}.
  • b) 8−2x≥08 - 2x \ge 08−2x≥0: x≤4x \le 4x≤4. Domain (−∞,4](-\infty, 4](−∞,4].
  • c) The cube root imposes no conditions; the denominator remains: x≠−1x \ne -1x=−1.
  • d) x2−3x−4≥0x^2 - 3x - 4 \ge 0x2−3x−4≥0, that is (x−4)(x+1)≥0(x - 4)(x + 1) \ge 0(x−4)(x+1)≥0: the parabola opens upwards and is positive outside the zeros. Domain x≤−1x \le -1x≤−1 or x≥4x \ge 4x≥4, that is (−∞,−1]∪[4,+∞)(-\infty, -1] \cup [4, +\infty)(−∞,−1]∪[4,+∞).
Exercise 6.2BasicEven or odd?

Decide whether these functions are even, odd or neither: f(x)=x4−2x2f(x) = x^4 - 2x^2f(x)=x4−2x2, g(x)=x3−4xg(x) = x^3 - 4xg(x)=x3−4x, h(x)=x2+xh(x) = x^2 + xh(x)=x2+x, k(x)=∣x∣+x2k(x) = |x| + x^2k(x)=∣x∣+x2, l(x)=xx2+4l(x) = \frac{x}{x^2 + 4}l(x)=x2+4x​.

Solution

All the domains are R\RR, which is symmetric.

  • f(−x)=x4−2x2=f(x)f(-x) = x^4 - 2x^2 = f(x)f(−x)=x4−2x2=f(x): even.
  • g(−x)=−x3+4x=−(x3−4x)=−g(x)g(-x) = -x^3 + 4x = -(x^3 - 4x) = -g(x)g(−x)=−x3+4x=−(x3−4x)=−g(x): odd.
  • h(−x)=x2−xh(-x) = x^2 - xh(−x)=x2−x, neither h(x)h(x)h(x) nor −h(x)-h(x)−h(x) (for example h(1)=2h(1) = 2h(1)=2 and h(−1)=0h(-1) = 0h(−1)=0): neither even nor odd.
  • k(−x)=∣−x∣+(−x)2=∣x∣+x2=k(x)k(-x) = |-x| + (-x)^2 = |x| + x^2 = k(x)k(−x)=∣−x∣+(−x)2=∣x∣+x2=k(x): even.
  • l(−x)=−xx2+4=−l(x)l(-x) = \frac{-x}{x^2 + 4} = -l(x)l(−x)=x2+4−x​=−l(x): odd.
Exercise 6.3BasicTwo composites

With f(x)=x2+1f(x) = x^2 + 1f(x)=x2+1 and g(x)=3x−2g(x) = 3x - 2g(x)=3x−2 compute (f∘g)(x)(f \circ g)(x)(f∘g)(x), (g∘f)(x)(g \circ f)(x)(g∘f)(x), (f∘g)(1)(f \circ g)(1)(f∘g)(1) and (g∘f)(1)(g \circ f)(1)(g∘f)(1).

Solution

(f∘g)(x)=f(3x−2)=(3x−2)2+1=9x2−12x+5(f \circ g)(x) = f(3x - 2) = (3x - 2)^2 + 1 = 9x^2 - 12x + 5(f∘g)(x)=f(3x−2)=(3x−2)2+1=9x2−12x+5.

(g∘f)(x)=g(x2+1)=3(x2+1)−2=3x2+1(g \circ f)(x) = g(x^2 + 1) = 3(x^2 + 1) - 2 = 3x^2 + 1(g∘f)(x)=g(x2+1)=3(x2+1)−2=3x2+1.

(f∘g)(1)=f(g(1))=f(1)=2(f \circ g)(1) = f(g(1)) = f(1) = 2(f∘g)(1)=f(g(1))=f(1)=2 (check: 9−12+5=29 - 12 + 5 = 29−12+5=2). (g∘f)(1)=g(f(1))=g(2)=4(g \circ f)(1) = g(f(1)) = g(2) = 4(g∘f)(1)=g(f(1))=g(2)=4 (check: 3+1=43 + 1 = 43+1=4). The two values are different: composition is not commutative.

Exercise 6.4BasicAn inverse

Find the inverse of f(x)=4x−3f(x) = 4x - 3f(x)=4x−3 and check that f−1(f(2))=2f^{-1}(f(2)) = 2f−1(f(2))=2.

Solution

fff is a non-horizontal line, so it is bijective from R\RR to R\RR. From y=4x−3y = 4x - 3y=4x−3 you get x=y+34x = \frac{y + 3}{4}x=4y+3​; swapping the names, f−1(x)=x+34f^{-1}(x) = \frac{x + 3}{4}f−1(x)=4x+3​.

Check: f(2)=8−3=5f(2) = 8 - 3 = 5f(2)=8−3=5 and f−1(5)=84=2f^{-1}(5) = \frac{8}{4} = 2f−1(5)=48​=2.

Exercise 6.5BasicA translation

Describe how the graph of y=(x+1)2−4y = (x + 1)^2 - 4y=(x+1)2−4 is obtained from that of y=x2y = x^2y=x2; find the vertex, the zeros and the point on the yyy-axis.

Solution

x+1x + 1x+1 inside the argument: 111 to the left; −4-4−4 outside: 444 down. The vertex moves from (0,0)(0, 0)(0,0) to (−1,−4)(-1, -4)(−1,−4).

Zeros: (x+1)2=4(x + 1)^2 = 4(x+1)2=4, that is x+1=2x + 1 = 2x+1=2 or x+1=−2x + 1 = -2x+1=−2: x=1x = 1x=1 and x=−3x = -3x=−3. yyy-axis: (0+1)2−4=−3(0 + 1)^2 - 4 = -3(0+1)2−4=−3, point (0,−3)(0, -3)(0,−3).

Exercise 6.6IntermediateDomains with fractions and roots

Find the domain of f(x)=x−2x+3f(x) = \sqrt{\frac{x - 2}{x + 3}}f(x)=x+3x−2​​ and of g(x)=x+4x−1g(x) = \frac{\sqrt{x + 4}}{x - 1}g(x)=x−1x+4​​.

Solution

fff: you need x−2x+3≥0\frac{x - 2}{x + 3} \ge 0x+3x−2​≥0, with x≠−3x \ne -3x=−3. The numerator is ≥0\ge 0≥0 for x≥2x \ge 2x≥2, the denominator is >0> 0>0 for x>−3x > -3x>−3; the fraction is positive or zero when they have the same sign: x<−3x < -3x<−3 or x≥2x \ge 2x≥2. The value −3-3−3 is excluded (it makes the denominator zero), 222 is included (it makes the numerator zero).

ggg: x+4≥0x + 4 \ge 0x+4≥0 and x−1≠0x - 1 \ne 0x−1=0, that is x≥−4x \ge -4x≥−4 with x≠1x \ne 1x=1: domain [−4,1)∪(1,+∞)[-4, 1) \cup (1, +\infty)[−4,1)∪(1,+∞).

Exercise 6.7IntermediateZeros and sign

a) Find the zeros and the sign of f(x)=x3−4x2+3xf(x) = x^3 - 4x^2 + 3xf(x)=x3−4x2+3x. b) Find the zeros of g(x)=xx+1−2x−2g(x) = \frac{x}{x + 1} - \frac{2}{x - 2}g(x)=x+1x​−x−22​.

Solution

a) f(x)=x(x2−4x+3)=x(x−1)(x−3)f(x) = x(x^2 - 4x + 3) = x(x - 1)(x - 3)f(x)=x(x2−4x+3)=x(x−1)(x−3): zeros 000, 111, 333. With the sign chart of the three factors: f(x)>0f(x) > 0f(x)>0 for 0<x<10 < x < 10<x<1 or x>3x > 3x>3; f(x)<0f(x) < 0f(x)<0 for x<0x < 0x<0 or 1<x<31 < x < 31<x<3.

b) Domain: x≠−1x \ne -1x=−1 and x≠2x \ne 2x=2. With the common denominator (x+1)(x−2)(x + 1)(x - 2)(x+1)(x−2), g(x)=0g(x) = 0g(x)=0 when x(x−2)−2(x+1)=0x(x - 2) - 2(x + 1) = 0x(x−2)−2(x+1)=0, that is x2−4x−2=0x^2 - 4x - 2 = 0x2−4x−2=0:

x=4±16+82=4±262=2±6x = \frac{4 \pm \sqrt{16 + 8}}{2} = \frac{4 \pm 2\sqrt6}{2} = 2 \pm \sqrt6x=24±16+8​​=24±26​​=2±6​

Neither of the two values is −1-1−1 or 222: the zeros are 2+62 + \sqrt62+6​ and 2−62 - \sqrt62−6​.

Exercise 6.8IntermediateA piecewise function
f(x)={x+3if x<−1x2+1if −1≤x≤12if x>1f(x) = \begin{cases} x + 3 & \text{if } x < -1 \\ x^2 + 1 & \text{if } -1 \le x \le 1 \\ 2 & \text{if } x > 1 \end{cases}f(x)=⎩⎨⎧​x+3x2+12​if x<−1if −1≤x≤1if x>1​

Compute f(−3)f(-3)f(−3), f(−1)f(-1)f(−1), f(0)f(0)f(0) and f(5)f(5)f(5); draw the graph; decide whether fff is continuous, what its range is, whether it is bounded and where it increases or decreases.

Solution

f(−3)=−3+3=0f(-3) = -3 + 3 = 0f(−3)=−3+3=0; f(−1)=1+1=2f(-1) = 1 + 1 = 2f(−1)=1+1=2; f(0)=1f(0) = 1f(0)=1; f(5)=2f(5) = 2f(5)=2.

At x=−1x = -1x=−1 the first piece reaches −1+3=2-1 + 3 = 2−1+3=2, the same value as f(−1)f(-1)f(−1); at x=1x = 1x=1 the second piece is 222, like the third. There are no jumps: fff is continuous.

Range: the first piece gives all the values less than 222, the second the values between 111 and 222, the third the value 222. Range (−∞,2](-\infty, 2](−∞,2]: fff is bounded above (the maximum is 222) but not below.

Increasing on (−∞,−1](-\infty, -1](−∞,−1], decreasing on [−1,0][-1, 0][−1,0], increasing on [0,1][0, 1][0,1], constant on [1,+∞)[1, +\infty)[1,+∞). It is not injective: f(1)=f(5)=2f(1) = f(5) = 2f(1)=f(5)=2.

Exercise 6.9IntermediateCounting solutions with the absolute value

Draw y=∣x2−2x−3∣y = |x^2 - 2x - 3|y=∣x2−2x−3∣ and use the graph to say how many solutions the equation ∣x2−2x−3∣=k|x^2 - 2x - 3| = k∣x2−2x−3∣=k has for k=2k = 2k=2, k=4k = 4k=4, k=5k = 5k=5.

Solution

x2−2x−3=(x−3)(x+1)x^2 - 2x - 3 = (x - 3)(x + 1)x2−2x−3=(x−3)(x+1): zeros −1-1−1 and 333, vertex (1,−4)(1, -4)(1,−4). Between −1-1−1 and 333 the parabola lies below the axis: flipped over, it becomes an arc with its highest point at (1,4)(1, 4)(1,4).

  • k=2k = 2k=2: the line y=2y = 2y=2 cuts the two outer branches and the arc twice: 444 solutions.
  • k=4k = 4k=4: it touches the arc only at its highest point and cuts the two outer branches: 333 solutions.
  • k=5k = 5k=5: it passes above the arc and cuts only the outer branches: 222 solutions.

Algebraic check for k=4k = 4k=4: x2−2x−3=4x^2 - 2x - 3 = 4x2−2x−3=4 gives x=1±22x = 1 \pm 2\sqrt2x=1±22​; x2−2x−3=−4x^2 - 2x - 3 = -4x2−2x−3=−4 gives (x−1)2=0(x - 1)^2 = 0(x−1)2=0, that is x=1x = 1x=1.

Exercise 6.10IntermediateA distance-time graph

The graph shows the distance sss from home, in km, of a car as a function of time ttt, in hours. Describe the journey; state where the function is increasing, decreasing or constant; is it continuous? Is it injective? Is it bounded?

Solution

In the first hour the car moves away from home up to 606060 km: the function is increasing on [0,1][0, 1][0,1]. From the first to the second hour it is stationary: constant on [1,2][1, 2][1,2]. Then it comes back to 202020 km from home: decreasing on [2,3][2, 3][2,3]. Finally it stops again: constant on [3,4][3, 4][3,4].

It is continuous: the position cannot “jump”, and the graph can be drawn without lifting the pen. It is not injective: for example the distance of 404040 km is reached twice, on the way out and on the way back. It is bounded: 0≤s≤600 \le s \le 600≤s≤60.

Exercise 6.11IntermediateUsing periodicity

fff is periodic with period 444, with f(1)=3f(1) = 3f(1)=3 and f(2)=−1f(2) = -1f(2)=−1. Compute f(9)f(9)f(9), f(−2)f(-2)f(−2), f(14)f(14)f(14) and f(−7)f(-7)f(−7).

Solution

You can add or subtract the period as many times as you like: f(9)=f(1+2⋅4)=f(1)=3f(9) = f(1 + 2 \cdot 4) = f(1) = 3f(9)=f(1+2⋅4)=f(1)=3; f(−2)=f(2−4)=f(2)=−1f(-2) = f(2 - 4) = f(2) = -1f(−2)=f(2−4)=f(2)=−1; f(14)=f(2+3⋅4)=f(2)=−1f(14) = f(2 + 3 \cdot 4) = f(2) = -1f(14)=f(2+3⋅4)=f(2)=−1; f(−7)=f(1−2⋅4)=f(1)=3f(-7) = f(1 - 2 \cdot 4) = f(1) = 3f(−7)=f(1−2⋅4)=f(1)=3.

Exercise 6.12Test levelProportionality from a table

For each row of values of yyy, decide whether yyy is directly proportional to xxx, inversely proportional, or neither; if there is a law, write it.

xxx222444555101010
yyy, row A101010555444222
yyy, row B55510101012.512.512.5252525
yyy, row C777111111131313232323
Solution
  • A: the products xyxyxy are always 202020: inverse proportionality, y=20xy = \frac{20}{x}y=x20​. For example for x=8x = 8x=8 you would have y=208=2.5y = \frac{20}{8} = 2.5y=820​=2.5.
  • B: the ratios yx\frac{y}{x}xy​ are always 2.52.52.5: direct proportionality, y=52xy = \frac{5}{2}xy=25​x.
  • C: neither the ratios (72≠114\frac{7}{2} \ne \frac{11}{4}27​=411​) nor the products (14≠4414 \ne 4414=44) are constant. The values grow by 222 for each unit of xxx: y=2x+3y = 2x + 3y=2x+3, linear but not proportional.
Exercise 6.13Test levelBounded or not?

Knowing that cos⁡x\cos xcosx takes all and only the values of the interval [−1,1][-1, 1][−1,1], decide whether these functions are bounded and find their range: a) cos⁡(x+5)\cos(x + 5)cos(x+5); b) cos⁡x−4\cos x - 4cosx−4; c) 1cos⁡x+2\frac{1}{\cos x + 2}cosx+21​; d) 1cos⁡x−1\frac{1}{\cos x - 1}cosx−11​.

Solution
  • a) It is a horizontal translation: the values taken do not change. Range [−1,1][-1, 1][−1,1], bounded.
  • b) Translation downwards by 444: range [−5,−3][-5, -3][−5,−3], bounded.
  • c) cos⁡x+2\cos x + 2cosx+2 takes the values of [1,3][1, 3][1,3], always positive; the reciprocal goes from 13\frac{1}{3}31​ (when the denominator is 333) to 111 (when it is 111). Range [13,1]\left[\frac{1}{3}, 1\right][31​,1], bounded.
  • d) Where cos⁡x=1\cos x = 1cosx=1 the denominator is zero and the function is not defined. Elsewhere cos⁡x−1\cos x - 1cosx−1 takes all the values of [−2,0)[-2, 0)[−2,0), always negative. The reciprocal is −12-\frac{1}{2}−21​ when the denominator is −2-2−2; when the denominator gets close to 000, the reciprocal is negative and as large as you like in absolute value. Range (−∞,−12]\left(-\infty, -\frac{1}{2}\right](−∞,−21​]: the function is bounded above (the maximum is −12-\frac{1}{2}−21​) but not below.

Consider f(x)=2x−1x+3f(x) = \frac{2x - 1}{x + 3}f(x)=x+32x−1​. Find the domain, the range and the inverse.

Solution

Domain: x≠−3x \ne -3x=−3. From y=2x−1x+3y = \frac{2x - 1}{x + 3}y=x+32x−1​: y(x+3)=2x−1y(x + 3) = 2x - 1y(x+3)=2x−1, that is xy+3y=2x−1xy + 3y = 2x - 1xy+3y=2x−1, so x(y−2)=−3y−1x(y - 2) = -3y - 1x(y−2)=−3y−1 and

x=−3y−1y−2=3y+12−yx = \frac{-3y - 1}{y - 2} = \frac{3y + 1}{2 - y}x=y−2−3y−1​=2−y3y+1​

You can solve for xxx for every y≠2y \ne 2y=2, and in only one way: the range of fff is R∖{2}\R \setminus \{2\}R∖{2} and fff is bijective from R∖{−3}\R \setminus \{-3\}R∖{−3} to R∖{2}\R \setminus \{2\}R∖{2}. Swapping the names: f−1(x)=3x+12−xf^{-1}(x) = \frac{3x + 1}{2 - x}f−1(x)=2−x3x+1​, defined for x≠2x \ne 2x=2.

Check at a point: f(0)=−13f(0) = -\frac{1}{3}f(0)=−31​ and f−1(−13)=−1+12+13=0f^{-1}\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right) = \frac{-1 + 1}{2 + \frac{1}{3}} = 0f−1(−31​)=2+31​−1+1​=0.

  1. What is the domain of f(x)=x+2x−3f(x) = \frac{\sqrt{x + 2}}{x - 3}f(x)=x−3x+2​​?

    First fff, then ggg: g(x−1)=(x−1)2g(x - 1) = (x - 1)^2g(x−1)=(x−1)2. x2−1x^2 - 1x2−1 is (f∘g)(x)(f \circ g)(x)(f∘g)(x), x3−x2x^3 - x^2x3−x2 is the product g(x)⋅f(x)g(x) \cdot f(x)g(x)⋅f(x), x2+x−1x^2 + x - 1x2+x−1 is the sum.
  4. If f(x)=3x+6f(x) = 3x + 6f(x)=3x+6, what is f−1(9)f^{-1}(9)f−1(9)?

    f−1(9)f^{-1}(9)f−1(9) is the xxx for which f(x)=9f(x) = 9f(x)=9: 3x+6=93x + 6 = 93x+6=9, so x=1x = 1x=1. It must not be confused with 1f(9)=133\frac{1}{f(9)} = \frac{1}{33}f(9)1​=331​.
  5. Which of these functions are odd?
    One or more correct answers
    Compute f(−x)f(-x)f(−x): (−x)3+(−x)=−(x3+x)(-x)^3 + (-x) = -(x^3 + x)(−x)3+(−x)=−(x3+x); 1−x=−1x\frac{1}{-x} = -\frac{1}{x}−x1​=−x1​; (−x)∣−x∣=−x∣x∣(-x)|-x| = -x|x|(−x)∣−x∣=−x∣x∣. On the other hand, x2+xx^2 + xx2+x is neither even nor odd and ∣x∣|x|∣x∣ is even.
  6. True or false: the function f(x)=x2f(x) = x^2f(x)=x2, from R\RR to R\RR, is injective.
    A counterexample is enough: f(−3)=f(3)=9f(-3) = f(3) = 9f(−3)=f(3)=9.

    It is decreasing on (−∞,0)(-\infty, 0)(−∞,0) and on (0,+∞)(0, +\infty)(0,+∞) taken separately, but −1<1-1 < 1−1<1 and f(−1)=−1<f(1)=1f(-1) = -1 < f(1) = 1f(−1)=−1<f(1)=1.
  8. The graph of y=(x−3)2+1y = (x - 3)^2 + 1y=(x−3)2+1 is obtained from that of y=x2y = x^2y=x2 by shifting it
    Inside the argument there is x−3x - 3x−3: 333 to the right (against the sign); outside there is +1+1+1: 111 up. The vertex goes to (3,1)(3, 1)(3,1).

    ∣x−2∣|x - 2|∣x−2∣ takes all the values ≥0\ge 0≥0; subtracting 333 you get all the values ≥−3\ge -3≥−3. The graph is a “V” with its vertex at (2,−3)(2, -3)(2,−3).

It increases for x≤0x \le 0x≤0 and decreases for x≥0x \ge 0x≥0.
  12. Which of these laws expresses a direct proportionality between xxx and yyy?
    Direct proportionality means a constant ratio yx\frac{y}{x}xy​: a line through the origin. y=4x+1y = 4x + 1y=4x+1 is linear but does not pass through the origin; the last two options are the same inverse proportionality.

    The cube root is defined for every real number, and x2+4≥4x^2 + 4 \ge 4x2+4≥4 is never zero. The option x≠±2x \ne \pm 2x=±2 confuses x2+4x^2 + 4x2+4 with x2−4x^2 - 4x2−4; the others treat the cube root like a square root.

Known errata in this material

In the material of this module we found a few errata, checked against the original pages and PDFs; the notes give the correct version.

  • Libro 6.1, translations: cos⁡(x2+1)\cos\left(\frac{x}{2} + 1\right)cos(2x​+1) is obtained from cos⁡x2\cos\frac{x}{2}cos2x​ by a translation of 2 units to the left, not one, because cos⁡(x2+1)=cos⁡x+22\cos\left(\frac{x}{2} + 1\right) = \cos\frac{x + 2}{2}cos(2x​+1)=cos2x+2​. In the same way, cos⁡(x2−1)\cos\left(\frac{x}{2} - 1\right)cos(2x​−1) is shifted 2 units to the right. The vertical shifts (±1\pm 1±1) are correct.
  • Soluzioni 6.1, exercise 1: the domain of f(x)=2x2−x−3f(x) = \sqrt{2x^2 - x - 3}f(x)=2x2−x−3​ is x≤−1x \le -1x≤−1 or x≥32x \ge \frac{3}{2}x≥23​, not x≤1x \le 1x≤1 or x≥32x \ge \frac{3}{2}x≥23​.
